Turns out its pretty meaningful because that's basically exactly what they are talking about, its part of what logjam was predicated on. They aren't attacking the encryption itself, they are talking about the DH used for key exchange. Because both sides of the exchange need to have the same 'Lpn', and because it takes such a long time to generate a "random" prime to begin with, everyone is using the same few primes EVERY time.

Logjam induced a connection to use 512-bit key exchange so it was much more vulnerable to the same basic idea, at which point you just wait and both parties happily tell you how to decrypt the actual traffic.

The crypto isn't broken in the sense that they could brute force any arbitrary ciphertext on a whim, but the overall end-to-end of the system to deliver that ciphertext in a way that can be understood on the other end is hijacked. So no, Amazon won't be emailing out movie keypairs for you to generate movies against the Amazon Binary Recombobulation Matrix any time soon.

You may find Tupper's Self Referential Formula interesting in regard to data construction with large primes. It outputs a plot chart bitmap of itself or any arbitrary bitmap with the right prime plugged in.
